question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
After Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls the Corrupted Conscience, and because of that, Analia also controls the Bane Alley Blackguard. Here's why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," and Analia's Lay Claim was cast targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience (an enchantment, which is a legal target for a permanent-enchanting Aura). When Lay Claim resolves, it becomes attached to Corrupted Conscience, and its effect gives control of that enchanted permanent — the Corrupted Conscience — to Analia [608.3c],[303.4].

Corrupted Conscience's own text says "You control enchanted creature," where "you" means whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience [303.4e],[110.2b]. Before Lay Claim resolved, Nico controlled Corrupted Conscience, so Nico was the "you" who controlled the enchanted Bane Alley Blackguard. Once Analia gains control of Corrupted Conscience via Lay Claim, the "you" in Corrupted Conscience's ability updates to Analia, so Analia now controls the enchanted creature, Bane Alley Blackguard.

Note that this is different from the more common case where you gain control of a creature that happens to have an Aura attached to it — in that case, per the Lay Claim ruling, gaining control of the creature does NOT give you control of the Aura enchanting it [Lay Claim ruling #0]. That's not what's happening here, though: Analia's Lay Claim targeted and gained control of the Aura itself (Corrupted Conscience), and it's Corrupted Conscience's own control-changing ability that then flows through to give Analia the creature, Bane Alley Blackguard, as a side effect.

Also note that attaching Corrupted Conscience remains legal and doesn't move — Lay Claim just changes who controls it, per rule 303.4e's principle that changing control of an Aura doesn't by itself change control of what it's attached to; it's specifically Corrupted Conscience's textual ability referencing 'you' that produces the follow-on control change of Bane Alley Blackguard.

This analysis assumes a standard two-player game; the rules provided don't include any multiplayer-specific wrinkle that would change this particular interaction, since it's about a single control-changing chain rather than choosing among multiple opponents.

question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, and it will be a 4/4.

Here's why: Alan now controls five enchantments — Iroas, God of Victory, the three other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself. That satisfies Starfield of Nyx's condition ("As long as you control five or more enchantments..."), so its ability applies: "each other non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Iroas, God of Victory is an enchantment (and not an Aura) other than Starfield of Nyx, so it qualifies.

This matters because Iroas, God of Victory's own text says "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Both effects are type-changing effects and are applied in layer 4 [613.1d]. Iroas, God of Victory's own devotion-based effect has been continuously applying since it entered the battlefield, but Starfield of Nyx's type-granting effect only begins applying once its condition is met (when the fifth enchantment, in this case Starfield of Nyx itself, is on the battlefield) — a later timestamp. As the layering rules illustrate with sequential type-setting effects on the same permanent (e.g., the Svogthos, the Restless Tomb example), later-applied layer-4 effects are layered on top of earlier ones [613.6]. Because Starfield of Nyx's effect explicitly makes Iroas, God of Victory a creature "in addition to its other types" — a phrasing that specifically preserves and adds to prior types rather than replacing them [205.1b, 300.2] — its later application restores/adds the creature type regardless of what Iroas, God of Victory's own ability set earlier in that same layer. So even though Alan's devotion to red and white is still well under seven (it only grows from 2 toward 3 or so once Starfield of Nyx's own {W} is added, nowhere near 7 — devotion is calculated the same way regardless [700.5a]), Iroas, God of Victory becomes a creature anyway, independent of its own devotion clause.

For power and toughness: Starfield of Nyx's ability sets base power and base toughness equal to the affected enchantment's mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, mana value 4, so its base power and toughness both become 4, making it a 4/4 (this layer-7b setting effect overrides its printed 7/4). Its other abilities (indestructible, granting menace, preventing damage to attacking creatures you control) are unaffected by any of this.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up as a 5/4 creature (with no first strike). Here's why:

Step 1 – Muraganda Petroglyphs alone: Grizzly Bears has no printed abilities, so Muraganda Petroglyphs' static ability ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") applies to it in layer 7c, making it 4/4. This is a continuously-checked condition, not a one-time snapshot — if Grizzly Bears ever gains an ability, it stops qualifying, and if it later has no abilities again, it starts qualifying again [611.3b] [613.4c].

Step 2 – Crowd's Favor resolves targeting Grizzly Bears: Crowd's Favor gives Grizzly Bears +1/+0 (layer 7c) and first strike (layer 6) until end of turn. Once Grizzly Bears has first strike, it now has an ability, so Muraganda Petroglyphs' condition ("no abilities") is no longer met and its +2/+2 stops applying. Layer 6 (ability-granting effects) is resolved before layer 7 (power/toughness effects) [613.1g], so by the time Muraganda Petroglyphs' condition is checked in layer 7c, Grizzly Bears already has first strike from Crowd's Favor. At this point Grizzly Bears is 2/2 base + 1/+0 = 3/2 with first strike.

Step 3 – Archetype of Courage resolves: Archetype of Courage's second static ability says "Creatures your opponents control lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." Grizzly Bears is controlled by an opponent of Archetype of Courage's controller, so this applies in layer 6: it strips away the first strike Crowd's Favor granted and prevents Grizzly Bears from having or gaining first strike for the rest of the effect's duration. Layer 6 is resolved in timestamp order — Crowd's Favor's first-strike grant has an earlier timestamp, then Archetype of Courage's removal/prevention effect (later timestamp) applies on top of it [613.7] [613.6] — so the net result after layer 6 is that Grizzly Bears has no abilities at all again.

Since layer 6 is fully resolved before layer 7 is evaluated [613.1g] [613.8], Muraganda Petroglyphs now sees a Grizzly Bears with no abilities once more, so its +2/+2 (timestamp from when it entered the battlefield, earlier than Crowd's Favor) reapplies in layer 7c: 2/2 base → +2/+2 (Muraganda Petroglyphs) = 4/4 → +1/+0 (Crowd's Favor, still in effect until end of turn) = 5/4.

So the final power/toughness of Grizzly Bears is 5/4, and it no longer has first strike (Archetype of Courage's card text explicitly overrides Crowd's Favor's grant for creatures controlled by its caster's opponents).

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
Yes — Murmuring Bosk is currently a creature (specifically a 1/1 green Saproling land creature), although it has stopped being a Forest and has become a Mountain instead.

Here's why. Both Life and Limb's "all Forests... are... creatures... in addition to their other types" effect and Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" effect are type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 [613.1d]. Within a layer, effects are applied in the order their sources became active, which here is the order given in the question: Life and Limb entered first, then Blood Moon.

Applying Life and Limb first: Murmuring Bosk's own type line already includes the land type Forest, so it is one of "all Forests" affected by Life and Limb. It becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types [205.1b] (this mirrors how Life and Limb turns each Forest into a Forest land creature, per the card's text and Life and Limb ruling #3, which confirms Forest and Saproling are correlated as land/creature subtypes respectively and don't cross-contaminate each other's card type).

Then applying Blood Moon: Murmuring Bosk has no "basic" supertype (Murmuring Bosk ruling #0 confirms it's a Forest but not a basic land, and 205.4c says only lands with the Basic supertype are basic lands), so it qualifies as a "nonbasic land" and Blood Moon turns it into a Mountain. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type like Mountain strips its old land type (Forest) and any abilities from its rules text or old land type, and grants the Mountain mana ability, but it explicitly does **not** remove card types or supertypes the land has from other effects [305.7]. question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Under the timestamp-based application of the layer system (the ordering method explicitly given in rule [613.7]), both the Sapseep Forest and the 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token end up as 1/1 green Land Creatures with the subtypes Mountain and Saproling (i.e., a "Land Creature — Mountain Saproling"), each carrying only the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" — they lose Sapseep Forest's printed rules text and its Forest mana ability, and gain nothing from being a "Forest" anymore.

Here is the layer-by-layer reasoning:

Both Life and Limb and Blood Moon are type-changing effects, so both apply in Layer 4 [613.1d, 613.6]. Life and Limb entered the battlefield before Blood Moon, so by straightforward timestamp order [613.7] Life and Limb's effect is applied first, then Blood Moon's.

1. Life and Limb applies first: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" [Life and Limb]. Sapseep Forest already has the land type Forest, so it becomes a land creature, adding the creature subtype Saproling (Forest is retained as a land subtype, correlated to its own type per [205.3c]). The Saproling token, which already has the creature subtype Saproling, gains the land type Forest in addition to its other types, becoming a land as well [Life and Limb ruling #1]. Because this is a type/subtype change applied "in addition to" existing types, rule [205.1b] confirms both permanents keep all their prior types/subtypes on top of the new ones. Life and Limb's color-setting (green, Layer 5) and power/toughness-setting (1/1, Layer 7b) parts of the same ability also lock onto both permanents and continue to apply going forward even as their types change further [613.6].

2. Blood Moon applies second (later timestamp): "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" [Blood Moon]. Both Sapseep Forest and the (now-land) Saproling token are nonbasic lands (neither has the supertype Basic), so per rule [305.7] each one's land subtype is set to Mountain, replacing Forest. This strips the old land type Forest, all abilities generated from the object's rules text and from its old land type (so Sapseep Forest loses "This land enters tapped," its {G}, {T} life-gain ability, and the {G} mana ability tied to being a Forest; the token loses the {G} mana ability it had only just gained from being a Forest), and each gains the Mountain mana ability, "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2]. Rule [305.7] also confirms this subtype-setting does not remove or add any card types or supertypes — so the creature type and green/1-1 characteristics granted by Life and Limb are untouched by Blood Moon.

Result: Sapseep Forest and the Saproling token are both 1/1 green Land Creatures with the type line "Land Creature — Mountain Saproling," each with only the ability "{T}: Add {R}." Neither has Forest's mana ability, Sapseep Forest's life-gain ability, or "enters tapped" anymore, since those were tied to rules text/old land type that Blood Moon stripped. As creatures gained from Life and Limb, they're subject to summoning sickness rules for activating {T} abilities if you haven't controlled them continuously since your turn began [Life and Limb ruling #0].

Rule [613.8] states that a dependency, if one exists, overrides timestamp order, but the provided rules don't include the specific criteria (613.8a–c) that define when two effects are dependent on each other. Because Blood Moon's "nonbasic lands" check and Life and Limb's "all Forests" check each potentially affect whether the other's condition is met on the Sapseep Forest, a dependency relationship might exist that could force Blood Moon's effect to be evaluated before Life and Limb's on that permanent specifically (which, if it removed the Forest type before Life and Limb ever checked it, could change whether Sapseep Forest becomes a creature at all). I can't resolve that possibility with the rules given here, so treat the answer above as the timestamp-order result, with a known open question about whether dependency changes it.

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Cinder Glade ends up as a plain nonbasic Land — Mountain (colorless, not a creature) with only the ability "{T}: Add {R}", and the 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token ends up as a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with the ability "{T}: Add {R}" — in both cases the permanent is a Mountain, not a Forest, and neither Forest becomes a Saproling-style creature-and-land via the Forest route once Blood Moon has touched it.

Why Cinder Glade loses its Forest side and its creature-hood: Cinder Glade is printed as Land — Mountain Forest with no "basic" supertype, so it's a nonbasic land [Nonbasic Land; 205.4c]. Blood Moon's text "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets its land subtype to the basic type Mountain. Per rule 305.7, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips it of its old land types and any abilities generated from its rules text, and grants the intrinsic mana ability for the new type — confirmed by Blood Moon's own ruling: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" [Blood Moon ruling #2]. Since Blood Moon entered the battlefield before Life and Limb, its effect is the one already shaping Cinder Glade's land type when Life and Limb's condition is checked. Life and Limb only affects things that currently are Forests or Saprolings [205.3c]; because Cinder Glade is no longer a Forest (it's just a Mountain now), Life and Limb's "all Forests... are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" clause has nothing to grab onto. So Cinder Glade stays a non-creature Land — Mountain, losing its old "{T}: Add {R} or {G}" ability and its "enters tapped unless..." clause, and gaining only "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, 305.7, Blood Moon ruling #2].

Why the Saproling token becomes a Mountain instead of a Forest: The token is a Saproling, so Life and Limb's effect applies to it directly — Life and Limb ruling #1 confirms "Saprolings enter the battlefield as land creatures," and ruling #3 confirms it gains the card types creature and land plus the subtypes Forest and Saproling, each correlated to the right card type per 205.3c and retained "in addition to its other types" per 205.1b. Because the token only becomes a land at all through Life and Limb's effect, Blood Moon's "nonbasic lands are Mountains" clause can only have something to act on once Life and Limb has already made it a (nonbasic) land — this is the standard way two type-setting continuous effects with this kind of chicken-and-egg relationship resolve, consistent with how rule 613.6 lets separate parts of overlapping effects each apply in their own layer to the same object. I'm flagging this as an assumption: the precise dependency rule that formally mandates "apply Life and Limb's land-granting first, then Blood Moon's Mountain-setting" for this token isn't among the rules I was given, so if a table ruling or a dependency rule dictated the opposite order, the token would instead stay a Forest land creature untouched by Blood Moon. Net result: a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}."

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite is currently a green Artifact Land Creature — Forest Saproling with power/toughness 2/2, and it keeps all of its own printed abilities (the "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" ability and its Craft ability) plus a new intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" mana ability from being a Forest.

Here's how the four effects stack up, applied through the layer system:

1) March of the Machines ("Each noncreature artifact is an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value") checks Ore-Rich Stalactite while it is still just a plain artifact, so it qualifies and turns it into an artifact creature. This is the exact pattern described in the Svogthos/"noncreature artifacts become 2/2 creatures" example in [613.6]: the type-change (layer 4) and the power/toughness-set (layer 7b, to its mana value — {1}{R} = mana value 2) are locked in as one effect and both continue to apply to Ore-Rich Stalactite even after later effects change its other characteristics.

2) Xenograft (naming Saproling) only affects "each creature you control," so it can't check in until after March of the Machines has made Ore-Rich Stalactite a creature. Once it is a creature, Xenograft adds the creature type Saproling to it "in addition to its other types."

3) Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") only affects Forests and Saprolings. It can't apply to Ore-Rich Stalactite until Xenograft has made it a Saproling. Once that's true, Life and Limb's layer-4 portion adds the land type Forest and the creature type Saproling (already present) "in addition to its other types," so the Artifact type is retained per the retention principle in [205.1b] and combined per [205.2b] and [300.2]. Per [205.3c] and [205.3i], Saproling is the creature-type subtype and Forest is the land-type subtype (Forest is also one of the five basic land types, [305.5], [305.6]), so having the Forest land type gives Ore-Rich Stalactite the intrinsic mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" under [305.6], on top of its own printed abilities (card text is never removed by these type-changing effects unless it says so).

4) Color and power/toughness: Life and Limb also sets Ore-Rich Stalactite's color to green (layer 5) — nothing else contests color, so it stays green. But Life and Limb's power/toughness-setting (1/1, layer 7b) and March of the Machines' power/toughness-setting (mana value, layer 7b) both apply to the same object in the same sublayer, and neither one's applicability depends on the other at that layer (both simply set a number unconditionally once they qualify, per the same continuing-effect logic in [613.6]). With no dependency between them in layer 7b, they're applied in timestamp order — Life and Limb entered before March of the Machines in this scenario — so March of the Machines, being the later-timestamped effect, is applied last and its value (2/2, Ore-Rich Stalactite's mana value) is what sticks.

Net result: Ore-Rich Stalactite is a green Artifact Land Creature — Forest Saproling, 2/2, still with its own restricted red mana ability and its Craft ability, plus the "{T}: Add {G}" ability granted by being a Forest.

Note on assumptions: this all assumes the stated enter-the-battlefield order (and thus timestamp order) — Ore-Rich Stalactite, then Life and Limb, then March of the Machines, then Xenograft — is exactly as given. If March of the Machines had instead entered before Life and Limb in a different sequence, the layer-4 "who qualifies whom" chain would still work the same way (since it's forced by what each effect's condition checks), but if Life and Limb's power/toughness-set had a later timestamp than March of the Machines', the final power/toughness would flip to 1/1 instead of 2/2.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Both Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs are currently nonbasic lands that also have the basic land type Mountain, and each still has its own printed mana ability in addition to the automatic Mountain ability. Humility does NOT stop Magus of the Moon's land-type effect from working, even though Magus of the Moon is a creature and Humility strips creatures' abilities.

Here's why: Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect, which is applied in the type-changing layer, while Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities" is applied in the ability-removing layer, which comes later in the layer sequence [613.1]. Magus of the Moon's status as a creature is fixed by its printed card type and doesn't depend on its own land-affecting ability, so there's no circular dependency between the two effects (unlike the classic Opalescence/Humility loop, where the source's creature-ness is itself created by the same ability being stripped). Because the type-changing layer is resolved before the ability-removing layer, Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" ability is still "there" when land types are calculated, so it does turn Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs into Mountains. Humility subsequently strips Magus of the Moon's own text (and sets its power/toughness to 1/1), but that happens too late to undo the type change that already occurred in the earlier layer. The order in which these permanents entered the battlefield doesn't change this outcome, since the two effects operate in different layers with no dependency between them.

Because a basic land type comes with an automatic mana ability under rule 305.6 ("An object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability '{T}: Add [mana symbol]'... even if the text box doesn't contain that text"), each land now also has an automatic '{T}: Add {R}' ability from being a Mountain. That's in addition to — not instead of — its own printed mana ability, because rule 305.6 only grants an ability, it doesn't take away a land's own printed rules text. Also, per rule 205.4c, having the basic land type Mountain doesn't make either land a basic land — a land is only basic if it has the supertype "basic," and neither of these does, so both remain nonbasic lands.

Furycalm Snarl: normally has no land subtype at all (per its ruling, "The 'Snarl' itself doesn't have any land subtypes"). Under Magus of the Moon it is now Land — Mountain, still nonbasic, with two mana abilities available: its own printed '{T}: Add {R} or {W}' plus the automatic '{T}: Add {R}' from being a Mountain (the {R} option is redundant with what it already had). Its "reveal a Mountain or Plains / else enters tapped" ability was a one-time enters-the-battlefield trigger that already resolved when it entered and doesn't affect its current characteristics.

Crosis's Catacombs: normally Land — Lair with '{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}.' Under Magus of the Moon, its land subtype Lair is replaced by Mountain (so it's now Land — Mountain, still nonbasic), and it keeps its own printed '{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}' ability plus the automatic '{T}: Add {R}' (again redundant, since it could already produce {R}). Its "sacrifice unless you return a non-Lair land" trigger already resolved when it entered — since it's stated to still be on the battlefield under Ainsley's control, Ainsley must have returned a non-Lair land rather than sacrificing it; that trigger doesn't affect its current characteristics either.

One timing note: this all assumes Magus of the Moon and Humility are both still on the battlefield with their printed text unmodified by anything else. If some other effect had removed Magus of the Moon's ability before it entered, or removed Humility before Magus of the Moon entered, the lands would simply keep their normal (non-Mountain) types and abilities instead.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying. Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability reads, "As long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, this creature has the full text of that card and has the text '{2}: Discard a card.'" Because Mistform Skyreaver is a creature card, that condition is met (Yixlid Jailer only strips abilities from cards in graveyards, it does not change their card types, so Mistform Skyreaver is still a creature card sitting on top of the graveyard) [Yixlid Jailer ruling #1], [113.10]. 

The key question is whether Volrath's Shapeshifter's 'full text' acquisition sees Mistform Skyreaver as it is currently modified (with Flying and its mana ability stripped by Yixlid Jailer's 'Cards in graveyards lose all abilities') or as it's printed. Rule [612.6] tells us that Volrath's Shapeshifter's 'full text' mechanic works like a copy effect for name, mana cost, color indicator, power, toughness, and text. Rule [707.2a] establishes that when something copies an object's text/abilities, it uses the object's *copiable* values — the values derived from the text printed on the object — and explicitly states that 'other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects) ... are not copied.' Yixlid Jailer's ability-removal effect is exactly this kind of non-copy, text-affecting continuous effect applied to Mistform Skyreaver while it sits in the graveyard; it is not part of Mistform Skyreaver's copiable values, so it doesn't get carried over into what Volrath's Shapeshifter acquires. Volrath's Shapeshifter therefore ends up with the printed text of Mistform Skyreaver — including Flying and its '{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn.' ability — plus its own granted '{2}: Discard a card.' ability [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Undefined characteristics not present on Mistform Skyreaver would fall back to Volrath's Shapeshifter's own card, but Flying is not undefined here, so it carries through normally [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #2].

So despite Yixlid Jailer's continuous ability-stripping effect on graveyard cards, Volrath's Shapeshifter does have flying (and the creature-type-changing activated ability) as long as Mistform Skyreaver remains the top card of the graveyard. This analysis applies the same regardless of how many players are in the game, since it turns only on Aiden's own graveyard and battlefield permanents, not on opponent count.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
After both spells resolve, Swab Goblin is a 4/4 red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny," a Kithkin, with Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities (none of them activated yet on this copy). Watchwolf is a 0/4 red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny," a Treefolk only, with no abilities at all.

Here's why. Mirrorweave reads "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn," targeting Figure of Destiny. "Each other creature" means every creature except Figure of Destiny itself, so Swab Goblin and Watchwolf are both turned into copies of Figure of Destiny, while Figure of Destiny is unaffected by its own spell and keeps whatever it currently is (an 8/8 flying first‑strike Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar from its own activated abilities).

Crucially, a copy effect only copies the *copiable values* of the target — the values derived from what's printed on the card (name, mana cost, color indicator, types, rules text, power/toughness), as modified only by other copy effects or by 'as ... enters'/'as ... is turned face up' P/T-setting abilities [707.2a, 707.2]. Figure of Destiny's own P/T- and type-changing abilities are activated abilities, not characteristic-defining abilities and not 'as enters' abilities, so the 4/4-Warrior and 8/8-Avatar states they create are 'other effects' that are explicitly *not* copied [707.2a] (this is exactly the Chimeric Staff/Clone example: a Clone copying an activated Chimeric Staff gets the artifact and its activation ability, not the temporary 5/5 creature state). So both Swab Goblin and Watchwolf become copies of the *printed* Figure of Destiny: a 1/1 red/white Kithkin named "Figure of Destiny" with its three unactivated {R/W}-cost abilities as rules text [707.2, 707.3].

This copy effect (layer 1) is applied, and then any other continuous effects already affecting each permanent (which are not copy effects and so aren't overwritten) continue to apply on top of the new copied characteristics [613.2a, 613.7, 613.8]:
- Swab Goblin had already resolved Pack's Favor's "Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn" before Mirrorweave was even cast. That +3/+3 keeps affecting the permanent regardless of what it's a copy of, so its new base 1/1 becomes 4/4 for the rest of the turn.
- Watchwolf is still enchanted by Lignify, and Lignify's static ability keeps functioning on the permanent it's attached to: "Enchanted creature is a Treefolk with base power and toughness 0/4 and loses all abilities." Lignify's own ruling confirms it overwrites characteristic-defining information like power/toughness and creature types no matter what the enchanted creature would otherwise be [Lignify ruling #5]. So after the Mirrorweave copy makes Watchwolf into a 1/1 Kithkin with Figure of Destiny's three abilities, Lignify immediately strips the Kithkin type down to just Treefolk, removes all three of those copied abilities, and resets its base power/toughness to 0/4.

Neither Lignify nor Pack's Favor changes the name, mana cost, or color the copy effect assigned, so both permanents are now named "Figure of Destiny" with mana cost {R/W} and are red/white in color.

Note on timing: this assumes Pack's Favor fully resolved (and its +3/+3 is already in effect) before Mirrorweave was cast, exactly as the question states; if the +3/+3 had instead been applied after Mirrorweave, the end result for Swab Goblin's power/toughness would be the same (4/4) since these are independent, non-conflicting effects in different layers.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a black Goblin Zombie, and yes, it gets Dralnu's Crusade's +1/+1, becoming a 4/2.

Here's why. Conspiracy's ability is a type-setting effect: "Creatures you control are the chosen type" sets Leopard-Spotted Jiao's creature subtype to Goblin, and per rule 205.1a, when an effect sets a subtype it replaces the object's existing subtypes from that set — so Leopard-Spotted Jiao loses "Beast" entirely and becomes just "Goblin." This matches the printed ruling on Conspiracy that affected creatures "lose all of their other creature types" [Conspiracy ruling #4].

Dralnu's Crusade's ability, "All Goblins get +1/+1" and "All Goblins are black and are Zombies in addition to their other creature types," is a continuous effect that checks whichever permanents currently qualify as Goblins. Continuous effects like this are continually and automatically applied by the game, with all resulting characteristic changes recalculated together [613.5] — the classic example being a creature that becomes white and immediately starts benefiting from a "white creatures get +1/+1" effect. Once Conspiracy's type-setting effect (layer 4, per 613.1d) makes Leopard-Spotted Jiao a Goblin, it qualifies for Dralnu's Crusade's blanket effect: it becomes black (layer 5), gains the Zombie subtype in addition to its other creature types (layer 4) — so its final subtype is Goblin Zombie — and gets +1/+1 (layer 7c), taking it from 3/1 to 4/2. This lines up with the printed ruling that a Goblin affected by Dralnu's Crusade is 'already a black Goblin Zombie... with +1/+1' rather than acquiring these piecemeal [Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0].

Assumption/caveat: working out exactly which same-layer type-changing effect (Conspiracy's type-set vs. Dralnu's Crusade's type-add) is applied 'first' when one effect's applicability depends on the other isn't fully spelled out in the rule numbers provided here — I'm relying on the general principle in 613.5/613.6 that continuous effects continually check current characteristics, which produces the result above (and matches the well-known real-world interaction between Conspiracy and 'Lord' effects). If you have the specific dependency rule (governing order of same-layer effects when one affects the other's applicability), it confirms this same outcome by making Conspiracy's type-set apply before Dralnu's Crusade's Goblin-check.

This analysis is for however many players are at the table; nothing about it changes between two-player and multiplayer games since it only involves objects controlled by Allison.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant becomes a 4/4. Duplicant's ability sets its power and toughness to "the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it" (Duplicant's own text). The last (and only) card exiled is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, whose own text states "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library" — since it's moving from the battlefield to exile, its three +1/+1 counters stay on it. Under rule 122.1a, a +1/+1 counter "on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield" adds directly to that card's power and toughness, and Skullbriar's own ruling confirms this explicitly (a Skullbriar with a +1/+1 counter in a non-battlefield zone such as the command zone is a 2/2). So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave sits in exile as a 4/4 (its printed 1/1 plus the three +1/+1 counters). Duplicant (ruling #0) sets its own base power and toughness equal to that of the last creature card exiled, so Duplicant's base power and toughness become 4/4. This differs from the Death's Shadow example in Duplicant's rulings (ruling #2), where a static ability that continuously recalculates power/toughness from an external value doesn't carry over — that's not what's happening here, because Skullbriar's counters are simply sitting on the physical card object itself (per rule 122.1a) rather than being generated by an active ability that needs to keep functioning in exile. Duplicant is still a Shapeshifter (per its own text) and also gains Skullbriar's creature types (Zombie Elemental) as long as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave remains the last creature card exiled with it.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands can only tap for {R} (red) once Magus of the Moon resolves — it loses its normal "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" ability entirely and gains only "{T}: Add {R}."

Here's why. Badlands is a nonbasic land with the printed land types Swamp and Mountain, giving it the ability "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" (Badlands ruling #3). Two continuous, static effects are now trying to rewrite its land type: Conversion's "All Mountains are Plains" and Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Both are type-setting effects, and rule [305.7] says that whenever an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land type(s) and old rules-text abilities and gains only the mana ability for the new basic type — this matches Badlands ruling #1 ("land type changing effects that change a dual land's land type will remove the old land types completely") and Magus of the Moon ruling #4 ("nonbasic lands lose any other land types and abilities they had").

Crucially, neither Conversion nor Magus of the Moon cares about the other's output to know whether it can apply: Conversion's effect doesn't add or remove the "basic" supertype (per [305.7]), so Badlands stays nonbasic no matter what type it currently has, meaning Magus of the Moon can always grab it; and Badlands starts out already printed as a Mountain, so Conversion can always grab it too. Because both effects are continuously re-checking and re-applying (Conversion ruling #0 stresses it's a genuinely continuous effect, not a one-time snapshot), the *last* one applied in the type-setting layer is the one whose result sticks.

I'm assuming the normal timestamp convention: Conversion has been in play and generating its effect since before Magus of the Moon was even cast, so Magus of the Moon's effect is the newer one and is applied after Conversion's when the game evaluates Badlands' characteristics. That means the final state is "Mountain" (Magus of the Moon's result), not "Plains" (Conversion's result), so Badlands' only mana ability is "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #4). Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying again. Fleetfeather Sandals's static ability grants "equipped creature has flying and haste," while Tightening Coils's static ability makes the enchanted creature "lose flying" as a continuous effect in the same layer (the ability-adding/removing layer). Under rule 613.7e, an Equipment receives a brand-new timestamp every time it becomes attached to an object, even if it's re-attached to the same creature it was already on. So when Adriel activates Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability and re-attaches it to Wandering Ones, the flying-and-haste-granting ability gets a fresh, later timestamp than Tightening Coils's -6/-0-and-lose-flying ability. Per rule 113.10c, when two effects add and remove the same ability, the most recent (latest timestamp) effect prevails — so Fleetfeather Sandals's grant of flying now applies after Tightening Coils's removal, and Wandering Ones has flying (and haste). This matches the Tightening Coils ruling that if flying is granted to the enchanted creature after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature will have flying — re-equipping counts as a new grant with a new timestamp. Note Wandering Ones also keeps the -6/-0 power/toughness reduction from Tightening Coils, since that's a characteristic-setting effect in a different layer (power/toughness), not affected by the timestamp race over the flying ability.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
After Titania's Song resolves, Soldevi Digger is a colorless Artifact Creature — Equipment with mana value 2, power/toughness 2/2, and it has no abilities at all (its own printed ability, and the abilities Bludgeon Brawl would grant, are all stripped away).

Here's why, working through the layer system (rule 613.1) with Bludgeon Brawl's timestamp older than Titania's Song's (Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield when Titania's Song was cast):

Layer 4 (type-changing): Bludgeon Brawl applies first (older timestamp). At that moment Soldevi Digger is still an ordinary noncreature, non-Equipment artifact, so Bludgeon Brawl's text 'is an Equipment' makes it gain the Equipment subtype. Then Titania's Song applies (newer timestamp): its effect is checked against Soldevi Digger's state as a noncreature artifact (the state it had before Titania's Song's own type-change took hold), so it qualifies and 'becomes an artifact creature.' This is the exact scenario described in the [613.6] example of 'All noncreature artifacts become 2/2 artifact creatures until end of turn' — the type-changing part locks onto the object and keeps applying to it in every later layer even after the object stops literally being a 'noncreature artifact.' Because Titania's Song only sets the card types (artifact, creature) and never names a subtype, the Equipment subtype Bludgeon Brawl already gave it is retained under [205.1a], since the artifact card type itself is never removed. So after layer 4, Soldevi Digger is 'Artifact Creature — Equipment.'

Layer 6 (granting/removing abilities): Bludgeon Brawl (older timestamp) grants equip {2} (X = Soldevi Digger's mana value, 2) and the static ability 'Equipped creature gets +2/+0.' Then Titania's Song (newer timestamp), whose effect — per the same [613.6] continuation logic — still applies to Soldevi Digger, causes it to 'lose all abilities.' Because this happens after Bludgeon Brawl's grant in timestamp order, it strips out Soldevi Digger's original activated ability ('{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library') as well as the equip ability and the +2/+0 static ability that Bludgeon Brawl had just granted. Rule [113.12] confirms these granted abilities are removable the same way any granted ability is — losing all abilities takes them away, even though the Equipment subtype itself (a characteristic set in layer 4, not an ability) is untouched.

Layer 7b (power/toughness-setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to Soldevi Digger's mana value, 2, giving it 2/2.

No color-changing effect is present, so Soldevi Digger remains colorless.

Note on ordering: this all assumes Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield before Titania's Song was cast, which the question states. If instead Titania's Song had been in play first and Bludgeon Brawl entered afterward, Bludgeon Brawl's ability grant (now the newer effect) would apply after Titania's Song's ability-loss in layer 6, so Soldevi Digger would end up with the equip {2} ability and the 'Equipped creature gets +2/+0' ability, but still no original activated ability and still 2/2 (and Bludgeon Brawl would still need Soldevi Digger to have been a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact at some point for its type-setting to apply, which it would not be once already turned into a creature — a genuinely trickier case not fully resolved by the rules given here).

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Until end of turn, Wayward Angel becomes a blue Frog creature with no abilities and with power/toughness 1/1 (base 1/1, no bonuses apply) — it is not black, has no flying, vigilance, trample, or upkeep-sacrifice trigger, and it loses the "Angel Horror" creature type.

Here's why. Wayward Angel's threshold clause ("As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, this creature gets +3/+3, is black, has trample, and has 'At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.'") is a single static ability of Wayward Angel itself [113.12] whose effects apply across several layers: color in layer 5, ability-granting in layer 6, and the +3/+3 power/toughness boost in layer 7c (compare the analogous multi-layer effect examples in [613.6]).

Turn to Frog says "Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1." This is also a compound effect: type-changing (layer 4, making Wayward Angel just a Frog, no longer Angel Horror), color-changing to blue (layer 5), ability-removal (layer 6), and setting base power/toughness to 1/1 (layer 7b) [613.4b], [Turn to Frog ruling #0].

Applying the layers in order:
- Layer 4: Wayward Angel's creature type is set to Frog (its own text overrides any prior type).
- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold effect (earlier timestamp, since Wayward Angel already had threshold active before Turn to Frog was cast) makes it black first; Turn to Frog's later-timestamp effect then overwrites that to blue [613.7], [Wayward Angel ruling #0]. Final color: blue.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Threshold's earlier-timestamp grant of trample and the upkeep-sacrifice ability is applied on top of Wayward Angel's printed flying and vigilance, but Turn to Frog's later-timestamp "loses all abilities" then strips everything the creature has at that point — including the threshold static ability itself, since it too is one of Wayward Angel's abilities [113.12]. Wayward Angel now has no abilities at all.
- Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 [613.4b], [208.4a].
- Layer 7c: Because the threshold ability was already removed in layer 6 (a layer that comes before 7c), it no longer exists to generate its +3/+3 effect by the time layer 7c is checked — a static, condition-checked ability that has been stripped can't produce effects in later layers. So no power/toughness bonus applies here.

Result: Wayward Angel is a blue Frog creature, base power/toughness 1/1, actual power/toughness 1/1, with no abilities, until end of turn. Since the generating ability is gone, this stays true even if the graveyard later drops below or stays at seven cards — there's no ability left to re-check the condition.

This all assumes Wayward Angel already had 7+ cards in its controller's graveyard (threshold active) at the moment Turn to Frog resolves, as stated in the question; if threshold had not yet been active when Turn to Frog resolved, none of this matters because Wayward Angel would already have been a plain 4/4 white creature with only flying and vigilance, and Turn to Frog would simply wipe those and set it to a 1/1 blue Frog the same way.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
After Ariella turns the manifested Wayward Angel face up, Wayward Angel becomes (for the remainder of the turn) a black creature named Wayward Angel with the type Frog, with flying, vigilance, and an active Threshold ability, base power/toughness 1/1 modified to 4/4 (1/1 + Threshold's +3/+3), trample, and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature." Its mana cost stays {4}{W}{W} (Turn to Frog never touches mana cost).

Here's why. While manifested, Wayward Angel is a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, text, types, color, or mana cost [701.40a][708.2a]. Turn to Frog resolves while it's still face down, targeting it and applying a continuous effect until end of turn that sets it to a blue creature named nothing-in-particular but typed "Frog", removes all its abilities, and sets its base power/toughness to 1/1 [Turn to Frog ruling #1]. Because the face-down permanent had no abilities/color/type of its own at that moment, this establishes Turn to Frog's effect with an early timestamp: blue color, Frog type, no abilities, base 1/1.

Then Ariella turns it face up. Per rule 708.8, its copiable values revert to Wayward Angel's real printed characteristics (name Wayward Angel, types Angel Horror, color white, base 4/4, abilities Flying, Vigilance, Threshold, mana cost {4}{W}{W}) — and per rule 708.8, Turn to Frog's still-active effect continues to apply to the now-face-up permanent. Crucially, this means Wayward Angel's real name, types, color and abilities are all newly "acquired" at the moment of flipping, which happens after Turn to Frog already resolved. The Turn to Frog rulings tell us exactly how such later-arriving effects interact with its own effect:
- Turn to Frog ruling #3: "If the affected creature gains an ability after Turn to Frog resolves, it will keep that ability." Wayward Angel's Flying, Vigilance and Threshold abilities reappear at the flip, which is after Turn to Frog resolved, so they are kept rather than being stripped by Turn to Frog's ongoing "loses all abilities" effect.
- Turn to Frog ruling #0: "Turn to Frog overwrites all previous effects that set... base power and toughness... Any power- or toughness-setting effects that start to apply after Turn to Frog resolves will overwrite this effect." Threshold's bonus is a +3/+3 modifier, not a new base-setting effect, so it doesn't overwrite Turn to Frog's 1/1 base — it simply applies on top of that base (as later, non-base-setting continuous effects do), giving a final 4/4 (Wayward Angel ruling #0 confirms Threshold's color change is a full color replacement, not an addition, matching how the color layer works below).
- Because Threshold (with its color-changing text) is likewise regained at the flip — after Turn to Frog resolved — its "is black" instruction is a later-arising, same-layer color-setting effect than Turn to Frog's "becomes blue," so black overwrites blue, consistent with Wayward Angel ruling #0 ("it is not white and black," i.e., Threshold's color effect fully replaces, not adds to, the prior color).
- Turn to Frog's type-setting ("becomes a ... Frog") is never contested by anything Threshold grants (Threshold doesn't change creature type), so the Frog type from Turn to Frog persists even after the flip; Wayward Angel's normal type Angel Horror does not return.

Putting it together via the layer system referenced in rule 613.1: type = Frog (Turn to Frog, uncontested), color = black (Threshold's later-arriving set-effect beats Turn to Frog's blue), abilities = Flying, Vigilance, Threshold (all regained after Turn to Frog resolved, so ruling #3 protects them from Turn to Frog's ongoing removal), and power/toughness = base 1/1 (Turn to Frog) modified by +3/+3 from Threshold = 4/4. Since Threshold's own graveyard condition (seven or more cards) is met, its trample and "sacrifice a creature" upkeep trigger are also active. All of this lasts until end of turn, when Turn to Frog's effect expires and Wayward Angel reverts to being governed only by its own printed text (still black if the graveyard threshold is still met at that time).

This analysis assumes the order given in the question — Turn to Frog resolves fully, and only afterward does Ariella take the turn-face-up special action — which is exactly the timestamp relationship that makes ruling #3 and #0 apply the way described above. If instead the permanent had somehow been turned face up before Turn to Frog resolved (not the case here), Turn to Frog's effect would have a later timestamp than Wayward Angel's own abilities, and it would simply overwrite everything (blue, Frog, no abilities, 1/1) with nothing from Threshold surviving.

This is a two-player-neutral interaction (nothing here depends on player count).

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret (it has no other creature type at the same time).

Here's why, working through the effects in play:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability, "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types," applies to every land on the battlefield, including itself. So Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth gains the land type Swamp (in addition to having no other land types) [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0].

2. Because it is now a Swamp, Kormus Bell's static ability "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands" applies to it — this is a layer 4 type-changing effect [613.1d] that is continually reapplied as long as the permanent qualifies as a Swamp, the same way Honor of the Pure keeps applying to anything that's white [613.5]. The "still a land" wording means Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth keeps its land card type, its Swamp/legendary status, etc. [205.1b, 205.4b]. Kormus Bell's effect itself grants no creature *type*, just the card type "creature."

3. Independently, the Vastwood Zendikon enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth makes "Enchanted land ... a 6/4 green Elemental creature. It's still a land." This is also a layer 4 effect and gives Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth the creature subtype Elemental (plus color and P/T effects in other layers), again retaining its land type per the "still a land" clause [205.1b; Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5].

4. Conspiracy (naming Ferret) says "Creatures you control are the chosen type," and its ruling states explicitly that "Affected spells, cards, and creatures lose all of their other creature types" [Conspiracy ruling #4]. Since Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is now a creature (via Kormus Bell and/or Vastwood Zendikon), Conspiracy's effect applies to it, overwriting its creature type(s) to just Ferret and stripping the Elemental type it got from Vastwood Zendikon. Card text and card-specific rulings override how a general rule would otherwise apply, so Conspiracy's explicit "loses all other creature types" ruling controls here even though Vastwood Zendikon's Elemental-granting effect has a later timestamp [613.9].

So the end result: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a legendary land creature (still a land, still legendary, still has the Swamp land type), and the only creature type it has is Ferret. It is not also an Elemental — Conspiracy's replacement effect removes that.

One caveat: the comprehensive rules include a specific 'dependency' rule (governing when one continuous effect's application depends on the results of another within the same layer) that isn't included in the rules text provided to me. I'm relying on Conspiracy's own ruling, which directly states the outcome (loss of all other creature types), rather than needing to derive the layer-4 ordering from first principles — so this answer doesn't depend on that missing rule.

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
After Blood Moon resolves, Raugrin Triome has only the land type Mountain — it loses Island and Plains (its printed types) as well as the extra Swamp and Forest types it had picked up from Prismatic Omen.

Here's why: Raugrin Triome never has the supertype "basic" (per [305.8]/[205.4c], a land is only "basic" if it has that supertype, regardless of its land types), so it remains a nonbasic land the whole time and Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies to it.

Before Blood Moon resolves, Prismatic Omen's continuous effect (which has an earlier timestamp, since it was already on the battlefield) is already making Raugrin Triome "every basic land type in addition to its other types" ([Prismatic Omen ruling #0]), so at that point Raugrin Triome has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

When Blood Moon enters, its type-setting effect has a later timestamp and applies on top of that. Rule [305.7] governs this: "If an effect sets a land's subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." Blood Moon's own ruling confirms this directly: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" ([Blood Moon ruling #2])

So Blood Moon strips away all of Raugrin Triome's prior land types — its native Island/Mountain/Plains subtypes and the additional basic types granted by Prismatic Omen — and replaces them with the single land type Mountain, along with the ability "{T}: Add {R}." Raugrin Triome's other characteristics (name, and the fact that it's not legendary or basic) are unaffected, per [Blood Moon ruling #1] and [Prismatic Omen ruling #1] — Blood Moon's text overrides how the general continuous-effect layering would otherwise leave multiple types on the land, since Blood Moon's later-timestamped type-setting effect controls under [305.7].

This assumes normal timestamp order: Prismatic Omen was already in play before Blood Moon was cast, so Blood Moon's effect is applied after (and on top of) Prismatic Omen's in the layer system. If instead Blood Moon had somehow been placed with an earlier timestamp, Prismatic Omen would apply afterward and Raugrin Triome would end up with all five basic land types again — but as described (Blood Moon cast after Prismatic Omen is already resolved), Mountain alone is correct.

question: Ariel controls [Frostboil Snarl] and [Blood Moon]. They cast [Prismatic Omen]. After it resolves, what land types does Frostboil Snarl have?
answer:
After Prismatic Omen resolves, Frostboil Snarl has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

Here's why: Frostboil Snarl itself has no land subtype at all (per Frostboil Snarl ruling #0, the "Snarl" cycle lands don't have any land types printed on them). Blood Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-setting effect (rule 305.7, Blood Moon ruling #2): since Frostboil Snarl is a nonbasic land (it lacks the basic supertype, per rules 305.8 and 205.4c), this effect sets its land subtype to just Mountain, replacing whatever land types it had (here, none), and grants the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}."

Prismatic Omen's ability, "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types," is an additive type-changing effect, not a replacing one (rule 305.7: "If a land gains one or more land types in addition to its own, it keeps its land types and rules text, and it gains the new land types and mana abilities"; see also Prismatic Omen ruling #0). Both effects apply in layer 4 (rule 613.1d), in timestamp order. Blood Moon's effect has the earlier timestamp (it was already on the battlefield), so it applies first, setting Frostboil Snarl's subtype to Mountain. Prismatic Omen, cast afterward, has a later timestamp and applies second, adding Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest in addition to Frostboil Snarl's current types. Since Frostboil Snarl already has Mountain from Blood Moon, the net result is that Frostboil Snarl now has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest, along with the mana abilities for each (Blood Moon's granted {T}: Add {R} for Mountain and Prismatic Omen's granted abilities for the other four colors, per Prismatic Omen ruling #0).

Note that Frostboil Snarl's own printed ability ("{T}: Add {U} or {R}") was already stripped away when Blood Moon set its type, since rule 305.7 says the land "loses all abilities generated from its rules text" when its subtype is set by an effect -- this is Blood Moon's card text overriding the general default of a land keeping its own printed abilities.

This answer assumes Prismatic Omen resolved while Blood Moon was already in play and unchanged; if Blood Moon somehow left the battlefield before Prismatic Omen resolved, Frostboil Snarl would simply have the five basic land types without ever having been set to Mountain-only in between, but the end result of five basic land types would be the same either way.

question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Winged Temple of Orazca ends up able to tap for any one of the five colors — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} — but it no longer has its own printed "add one mana of any color" ability.

Here's why. Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic land (it has no basic land type printed on it), so Blood Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies to it. Per rule [305.7] and [Blood Moon ruling #2], setting a land's subtype to a basic land type (here, Mountain) makes it lose its old land type and "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land" — so Winged Temple of Orazca's own printed abilities (its any-color tap ability and its flying/pump activated ability) are wiped out, and it gains the land type Mountain plus the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" (per [305.6] and [Mountain]).

However, rule [305.7] also explicitly notes that this type-setting effect "doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects." Prismatic Omen's static ability, "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types," is exactly such another effect: per [305.7]'s rule for additive type effects, "if a land gains one or more land types in addition to its own, it keeps its land types and rules text, and it gains the new land types and mana abilities," and [Prismatic Omen ruling #0] confirms your lands "gain the mana ability of each basic land type." Because those Plains/Island/Swamp/Forest mana abilities come from Prismatic Omen (an effect other than Winged Temple of Orazca's own rules text or its old land type), Blood Moon's wipe-and-set effect does not strip them away, regardless of which effect you consider "first" — the note in [305.7] protects abilities granted by other effects from that removal.

So Winged Temple of Orazca ends up with the land types Mountain, Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest, and correspondingly the five basic mana abilities "{T}: Add {W}," "{T}: Add {U}," "{T}: Add {B}," "{T}: Add {R}," and "{T}: Add {G}" (the {R} one effectively duplicated, since both Blood Moon's Mountain type and Prismatic Omen's added Mountain type grant it). Since each of these is a {T} ability, tapping Winged Temple of Orazca lets you choose only one of the five colors per activation, just like any other land — it can't produce more than one color at once.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a Land Creature with the type line Land Creature — Forest Island Vedalken Wizard Saproling.

Here's why. Realmwright's printed text is "Lands you control are the chosen type [Island] in addition to their other types" — this only affects things that are already lands. Arcane Adaptation's text is "Creatures you control are the chosen type [Saproling] in addition to their other types" — this affects creatures, and Realmwright is a Creature — Vedalken Wizard, so it applies directly: Realmwright gains the Saproling subtype, becoming Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling. Life and Limb's text is "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" — once Realmwright has the Saproling subtype (from Arcane Adaptation), it qualifies as one of "all Saprolings," so Life and Limb makes it a land with the Forest subtype (and sets it to green, 1/1, though those aren't asked about here). Only after Realmwright itself becomes a land does its own ability ("Lands you control are Island in addition to their other types") have anything to grab onto — since Realmwright now controls a land (itself), that ability adds the Island subtype to itself as well.

All of this happens in Layer 4 (type-changing effects) per [613.1d]. So the dependency system overrides timestamp order, and the effects are applied in the order Arcane Adaptation → Life and Limb → Realmwright's own ability, exactly as described above (this mirrors the Svogthos-style self-referential resolution discussed under [613.6]).

Because all three effects use "in addition to their other types" language rather than "becomes" (a replacing type-set effect), Realmwright keeps every type and subtype it had before, per [205.1b] and [613.6]. Per [205.3c], each subtype stays correlated to the right card type: Forest and Island are land types, Vedalken, Wizard, and Saproling are creature types. So the final result is: card types Land and Creature; land subtypes Forest and Island; creature subtypes Vedalken, Wizard, and Saproling.

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token created by Helm of the Host's triggered ability will be legendary, because Leyline of Singularity's static ability adds the legendary supertype independently of the copy effect that says the token "isn't legendary."

Here's why: Helm of the Host's ability creates "a token that's a copy of equipped creature, except the token isn't legendary." That exception is part of the copy effect itself, so as the copiable characteristics are established, the resulting token's copiable values do not include the legendary supertype (Helm of the Host ruling #3). Normally, that would mean the token stays non-legendary even if it copies a legendary creature.

However, Leyline of Singularity says "All nonland permanents are legendary." This is a separate continuous effect that grants the legendary supertype to every nonland permanent, and per rule [205.4b], "an object's supertype is independent of its card type and subtype... When an object gains or loses a supertype, it retains any other supertypes it had." Leyline of Singularity's own ruling makes this explicit for exactly this kind of situation: "Adding a supertype doesn't overwrite other supertypes. Each nonland permanent will be legendary in addition to its other supertypes" (Leyline of Singularity ruling #0). So even though the Helm of the Host token's copy effect sets its copiable value to non-legendary, Leyline of Singularity's blanket effect still adds the legendary supertype to it on top of that — the two effects don't conflict, they stack, and the token ends up legendary.

One consequence worth noting: since the original Awoken Demon (equipped with Helm of the Host) is also made legendary by Leyline of Singularity, and the token copies its name "Awoken Demon" (per [111.4], a copy token takes the copied permanent's name), Ainsley would now control two legendary permanents both named Awoken Demon. That triggers the legend rule [704.5j], and Ainsley must choose one to keep, putting the other into the graveyard.

Assumption: this answer assumes Ainsley is playing a normal two-player or multiplayer game where Ainsley alone controls both Awoken Demon and the resulting token; the legend rule as stated applies per-player regardless of player count, so this doesn't change between two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
Assuming Dryad of the Ilysian Grove has been on the battlefield since before Blood Moon was cast (so Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's static ability has an earlier timestamp than Blood Moon's), here is what each land looks like once Blood Moon resolves:

**Snow-Covered Island** (already has the supertype "basic"): Blood Moon only affects "nonbasic lands" [305.7 note is about setting subtype; the classification comes from 205.4c: "Any land with the supertype 'basic' is a basic land... Any land that doesn't have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type."]. Since Snow-Covered Island has the basic supertype, Blood Moon does not touch it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect ("Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types") still applies, so Snow-Covered Island becomes a Basic Snow Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest, keeping its own "{T}: Add {U}" and gaining "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", and "{T}: Add {G}" [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0]. It keeps both the Basic and Snow supertypes [205.4b, Snow-Covered Island ruling #0].

**Mountain** (a basic land): Same logic — it has the basic supertype, so Blood Moon doesn't apply to it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove adds the other four basic types on top of its existing Mountain type, so it becomes a Basic Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest with all five basic mana abilities ("{T}: Add {W}/{U}/{B}/{R}/{G}").

**Study Hall** (a plain Land with no basic supertype): This is a nonbasic land [205.4c], so Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies to it. Under 305.7, an effect that sets a land's subtype to a basic land type strips the land of its old land type(s) (including any types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove had added, since Study Hall never gained the "basic" supertype and stayed nonbasic throughout) and all abilities generated from its rules text — so it loses its own "{T}: Add {C}" and its "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color..." ability. It becomes just Land — Mountain with the single intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, Mountain]. It remains nonbasic (Blood Moon's effect doesn't grant the basic supertype) [205.4c, 205.4b].

**Dryad Arbor** (Land Creature — Forest Dryad, with no "Basic" supertype on its type line): Even though it has the basic land type Forest, it lacks the supertype "basic," so per 205.4c it counts as a nonbasic land. Blood Moon therefore affects it too. Its card types (Land, Creature) and creature type (Dryad) are untouched — setting a land's subtype doesn't add or remove card types [305.7], and this matches the precedent that Dryad Arbor "continues to be a green Dryad creature" when changed into another basic land type [Dryad Arbor ruling #2, ruling #0]. Its color stays green via its color indicator, which applies in every zone [Dryad Arbor ruling #3]. Its land type is stripped of Forest (and of the other basic types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove had added) and set to just Mountain, so it loses "{T}: Add {G}" and gains "{T}: Add {R}" [305.7, Mountain]. End result: a 1/1 green Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still affected by summoning sickness and still not a spell [Dryad Arbor ruling #4], with only "{T}: Add {R}".

To summarize the mechanism: layer 4 applies Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's type-adding effect first (earlier timestamp), giving every land you control all five basic land types in addition to its other types; Blood Moon's type-setting effect then applies afterward, but only to lands that are still nonbasic (lack the "basic" supertype) — and having a basic land type added by Dryad of the Ilysian Grove does not make a land basic [205.4c]. So true basic lands (Snow-Covered Island, Mountain) end up with all five basic types and all five mana abilities, while nonbasic lands (Study Hall, Dryad Arbor) get overridden into plain Mountains, keeping only whatever supertypes/card types/creature types they already had.

If instead Blood Moon had been cast and resolved before Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered the battlefield, the timestamp order would flip: Blood Moon's effect (earlier) would apply first, then Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect (later) would try to add all five basic types on top. Since Study Hall and Dryad Arbor would already have been set to just Mountain and are still nonbasic, Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's later effect would still add the other four basic types to them (Dryad's effect isn't restricted to basic lands) — so the final state would actually be the same for all four lands, because Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's ability re-adds all basic types regardless of timestamp, and Blood Moon's set effect only checks nonbasic status, not land type. The only lands whose supertype status doesn't change are checked continuously, so the outcome described above holds regardless of casting order in this particular case.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Direct answer: Nico's Thespian's Stage (the one already copying Temple of Triumph) gets gutted by Alpine Moon — it keeps the name "Temple of Triumph" but loses all its land types and all its abilities (including its own copy-ability), and instead just has "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Alayna's newly-activated second Thespian's Stage, by contrast, becomes a full, functional copy of Temple of Triumph (name "Temple of Triumph," enters-tapped/scry-1 text present but not re-triggering, "{T}: Add {R} or {W}") and it also keeps its own copy ability, because Alpine Moon never touches it.

Why: Alpine Moon's own text (card data) says "Lands your opponents control with the chosen name lose all land types and abilities, and they gain '{T}: Add one mana of any color.'" This is a continuous effect that checks, on an ongoing basis, which lands an opponent of Alayna currently controls that are named "Temple of Triumph." When Nico's Thespian's Stage became a copy of Temple of Triumph, it copied Temple of Triumph's name along with its other copiable characteristics [707.3, 707.9b, 707.9c] (Thespian's Stage's own ability only adds an exception that it keeps its copying ability — it doesn't except the name from being copied [Thespian's Stage ruling #0]). So Nico's Thespian's Stage really is named "Temple of Triumph," and since (assuming a two-player game) Nico is Alayna's opponent, Alpine Moon's continuous effect applies to it: it loses all land types (it had none from Temple of Triumph anyway) and *all* its abilities — that includes the retained "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" clause, since that's still just an ability on the object — and gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" in their place. Nico's Thespian's Stage can therefore no longer be activated to copy anything else.

When Alayna then activates her own Thespian's Stage targeting the actual Temple of Triumph land, the copy effect gives her Thespian's Stage the copiable values of Temple of Triumph — the printed characteristics (as modified only by other copy effects), not the after-the-fact ability/type removal that Alpine Moon might be layering onto whichever permanent(s) it's hitting [707.3, 707.9b, 613.1c]. So Alayna's Thespian's Stage becomes a normal copy of Temple of Triumph, keeping its own copy-ability per its "except it has this ability" clause [707.9c]. Crucially, even though this new copy is also now literally named "Temple of Triumph," Alpine Moon still doesn't strip it, because Alpine Moon only affects lands *Alayna's opponents* control — and Alayna controls this Thespian's Stage herself. So it keeps enters-tapped/scry-1 text (inert now, since it's not actually entering the battlefield — no ETB abilities re-trigger from becoming a copy [Thespian's Stage ruling #1]), "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and its own copy ability, fully intact.

A couple of housekeeping notes from Thespian's Stage's rulings: neither Thespian's Stage untaps just from becoming a copy [Thespian's Stage ruling #2], and any counters or other non-copiable effects on the original Temple of Triumph aren't copied either [Thespian's Stage ruling #3].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Alpine Moon fully resolves (and its named-land effect is already active) before Alayna's second Thespian's Stage activation resolves, exactly as the question's sequence states. If instead the activation somehow resolved first, the outcome for what gets copied wouldn't change (copiable values are unaffected by Alpine Moon regardless of order), but Nico's original Thespian's Stage would only start losing its abilities once Alpine Moon actually resolves.

Multiplayer note: all of the given rules here are stated in a way that doesn't depend on exactly two players, but Alpine Moon's own wording, "lands your opponents control," means in a multiplayer game it would hit *every* opponent of Alayna's who controls a land named "Temple of Triumph" (including any other players' Thespian's Stage copies of it), not just Nico's — while any Temple of Triumph-named land Alayna herself controls, including her own Thespian's Stage, is always safe. No other multiplayer-specific rule changes this interaction.
