question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Result: Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature and becomes just a green enchantment. It keeps Kenrith's Transformation's "loses all abilities" effect, its base power/toughness of 3/3 (which no longer matters because it isn't a creature), and its green color, but it loses the creature card type and the Elk creature type.

Here's why. Both Kenrith's Transformation and One with the Stars are type-changing continuous effects, so they're applied in layer 4, in timestamp order, unless a dependency exists [613.7, 613.8]. Nothing about how One with the Stars' effect works depends on the specific source of Thraben Purebloods' card types — it just cares what card types are present when it's applied — so this is an ordinary timestamp case like the flying example in [613.9], not a dependency case.

Kenrith's Transformation attached to Thraben Purebloods first, so its layer‑4 effect ("is a green Elk creature ... loses all other card types and creature types") applies first: Thraben Purebloods becomes Creature — Elk with no other card types [Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3]. One with the Stars attaches afterward, giving it a later timestamp, so its layer‑4 effect ("Enchanted permanent is an enchantment and loses all other card types") applies second and overrides the result: Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment and loses the creature card type it had just gained. Because it loses the creature card type, it also loses the Elk subtype tied to that card type [One with the Stars ruling #2], the same way losing a card type strips its associated subtypes per the general rule on retaining/losing types [205.1b].

The other parts of Kenrith's Transformation still apply in their own layers per [613.6]: its color-setting effect (layer 5) keeps Thraben Purebloods green, its ability-removal effect (layer 6) keeps it with no abilities, and its base power/toughness-setting effect (layer 7) still sets 3/3, though that's meaningless now since the permanent is not a creature.

Note on order: this all assumes Kenrith's Transformation's timestamp is earlier (it was attached first, as stated). If the attachment order were reversed, the later-timestamped effect would be Kenrith's Transformation's, and it would re-establish Thraben Purebloods as a green Elk creature again, since its own "is a ... creature" wording is also a card-type-setting effect.

One thing the provided rules don't cover: whether Kenrith's Transformation itself would later be put into the graveyard because Thraben Purebloods is no longer a legal thing for it to enchant (its enchant ability says "Enchant creature"). That's governed by a state-based action rule that isn't included in the rules given to me, so I can't confirm that part with citation.

cited_text.613.9: One continuous effect can override another. Sometimes the results of one effect determine whether another effect applies or what another effect does. Two effects are affecting the same creature: one from an Aura that says “Enchanted creature has flying” and one from an Aura that says “Enchanted creature loses flying.” Neither of these depends on the other, since nothing changes what they affect or what they’re doing to it. Applying them in timestamp order means the one that was generated last “wins.” The same process would be followed, and the same result reached, if either of the effects had a duration (such as “Target creature loses flying until end of turn”) or came from a non-Aura source (such as “All creatures lose flying”). rewrite_queries: When a creature is enchanted by multiple Auras simultaneously, including both Kenrith's Transformation and One with the Stars, what are the effects of those Auras and how do they interact with each other?
answer_gold:
Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment with no abilities and with the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an illegal target and is put into the graveyard. Thraben Purebloods then regains all characteristics except its type is only enchantment. State-based actions are checked again. Nothing happens, and Allen gets priority.

This is an interaction of continuous effects, so the layers will need to be considered. In this case, no changes occur until layer four. There are two effects occurring in this layer, so timestamps will need to be considered. Since Kenrith's Transformation was attached first, Thraben Purebloods maintains its status as a creature. Then, One with the Stars turns Thraben Purebloods into an enchantment and removes all other types. Thraben Purebloods is changed to the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation in layer five. Thraben Purebloods loses all abilities in layer six due to Kenrith's Transformation. Lastly, Thraben Purebloods has its power and toughness set to the values stated in Kenrith's Transformation in layer seven. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an enchantment and is put into the graveyard. State-based actions are checked again, and nothing happens.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The merged permanent stays face down and has only the vanilla face-down characteristics: a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no creature types, and no abilities (and no mana cost). Putting the manifested card on top means it is the topmost component of the mutated permanent, and because a merged permanent's status (face up/face down) is determined by its topmost component, the whole permanent counts as face down.

Here's why: Soul Summons manifests the top card of Avery's library face down as a 2/2 creature. When the mutate cost of Trumpeting Gnarr is cast targeting that manifested creature and Trumpeting Gnarr resolves, instead of entering the battlefield on its own it merges with the target creature, becoming one merged permanent represented by both cards [702.140c][608.3d]. Avery, as the mutating spell's controller, chooses whether Trumpeting Gnarr goes on top of or underneath the manifested creature [702.140c]; here Avery keeps the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr's card goes on the bottom.

A mutated permanent normally derives its power/toughness, color, types, name, and mana cost from whichever card or token is on top, while gaining the abilities of every component card [702.140e]. But because the topmost component here is face down, the merged permanent's face-up/face-down status is set by that topmost component [730.2e], and a face-down permanent's characteristics are fixed regardless of what card is actually underneath it — a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. This mirrors how a face-down creature that becomes a copy of another creature still remains a vanilla 2/2 with no name, types, abilities, or mana cost even though the card it copied has all of those things [707.3]. The same principle applies to merging: Trumpeting Gnarr's card is still one of the components representing the permanent, but its abilities and characteristics don't surface while the permanent is face down.

If Avery had instead chosen to put Trumpeting Gnarr's spell on top (manifested creature on the bottom), the result would be different: the merged permanent would be face up, would have Trumpeting Gnarr's own characteristics (a green/blue 3/3 Beast named Trumpeting Gnarr) as the topmost card, and would have the abilities of both components [702.140e][730.2e].

This merged, face-down permanent could later be turned face up under whatever rule lets its topmost card be turned face up (e.g., the original manifest ability, if that card is a creature card, by paying its mana cost); at that point it would take on that card's real characteristics as the new topmost face-up component, plus the abilities of both components.

This answer assumes a standard two-player or multiplayer game context isn't otherwise relevant here, since nothing about turn order or opponents affects how mutate/merging characteristics work.
